question: Why do newborn blood-spot programmes accept many false alarms for every baby who is truly affected?
answer: Because the two mistakes cost different amounts. Missing a baby with a treatable metabolic disorder can mean lifelong brain damage; a false alarm costs a retest and a frightening week for the parents. So cut-offs are set to catch nearly every case, and in many US states false alarms outnumbered true cases many times over.
move: Where you set an alarm depends on which mistake you can least afford.
ask: In my own decisions, which mistake costs me more, missing something or a false alarm, and have I set my worry to match?
reference: Tarini, Christakis & Welch, State newborn screening in the tandem mass spectrometry era: more tests, more false-positive results, Pediatrics, 2006
